Python interop

Source: vignettes/interop.qmd

The channel speaks a language-agnostic wire protocol, so the peer at the other end does not have to be R. pymizu is the Python binding of the same shared-memory core, and a channel connects the two directly. Pass the peer program as a source string (instead of a quoted expression) and set the launcher to mizu_py_launcher(), which spawns python3 -m pymizu.child — probing for the interpreter and pymizu before the channel is created. Here a Python echo loop, mirroring the R one in Channels (runs when a python3 with pymizu and NumPy installed is on the PATH):

library(mizu)

ch <- mizu_channel(
  "
import pymizu
while True:
    x = ch.recv(30)
    if pymizu.is_sentinel(x):
        break
    ch.send(x * 2)
",
  launcher = mizu_py_launcher()
)

mizu_send(ch, c(1.5, 2.5, 3.5))
mizu_recv(ch, timeout = 5)
#> [1] 3 5 7
mizu_close(ch)

Atomic vectors cross without serialization: an R numeric, integer, or raw vector arrives in Python as a NumPy float64, int32, or uint8 array, and the same dtypes travel back the other way. An integer64 vector crosses as a NumPy int64 array both ways — bit64’s exact layout, constructed without bit64 — with NA at INT64_MIN in each direction. A large vector arrives as a zero-copy read-only view over the shared pages — the same ALTREP mechanism as between R processes, surfaced on the Python side as a NumPy array that maps the region. On a channel, a contiguous vector below 256 KB instead travels as one copy into the channel’s spill arena — cheaper than region machinery at that size — and crosses as a view from 256 KB; the 32 KB floor applies everywhere else (pools, strings, frames, dim and strided arrays). Strings cross as strings in both directions; NA_character_ reads as None in Python, and None comes back as NULL. A large Python list[str | None] arrives as a zero-copy character-vector view over the shared pages — None as NA_character_, an empty string as "" — one layout write, no copy or parse; below the zero-copy floor (32 KB) the list crosses by value.

Scalars, lists, and dicts with string keys cross both ways as R’s own logical/integer/double/complex/character/list values. A Date arrives as datetime64[D], a POSIXct as naive datetime64[us], a factor as list[str | None] (a dictionary-encoded column inside a frame), and a matrix as a Fortran-order array — the data never transposes. A large numpy array arrives as a zero-copy matrix view over the shared pages in any memory order — F order, C order, or strided — one layout write, no copy or parse, and a large datetime64 array crosses the same way as a POSIXct or Date view (NaT as NA). A large nested Python tree of lists, dicts, arrays, and strings arrives as a zero-copy list view over one shared region, and a view nested inside one crosses by reference — only its region’s name moves, and R resolves it to a view of the original region. A difftime arrives as timedelta64[us], NA as NaT — and timedelta64 arrays of any non-calendar unit travel back as a difftime; units cross by value and normalize to seconds on a round trip. A POSIXlt, a character matrix, a named character vector, and S4 objects stay on R’s side: sending one on a Python channel raises at mizu_send().

Labels cross with the values they name: a named vector keeps its names (an unmodified round trip is identical()), and a matrix or array keeps its dimnames — axis names included, so a table object arrives with its class and every axis label intact. On the Python side these arrive as pymizu.DimArray, an ndarray subclass carrying the labels; NumPy operations drop them rather than risk mislabeling reshaped data, so a modified array comes back as a plain array — re-attach labels in Python and they ride back. A labeled array used as a cross-language map’s x rides the raw-bytes section and drops its labels there — the same honest-loss rule as a same-language send.

A data frame crosses as a pymizu.Frame — column dict on one side, pl.from_arrow(f) / pa.table(f) on the way into polars or pyarrow — and a polars, pyarrow, or pandas frame arrives back as a data.frame. Past the zero-copy floor (32 KB of layout) the frame travels as one shared-memory region both directions: no copy, no parse, numeric columns read in place. An unmodified R → polars → R round trip moves zero payload bytes at all — the return hop is a reference to the region R itself staged. The full contract, with the NA-sentinel and widening rules per dtype, is the dtype matrix in the pymizu README; a value outside the portable subset raises at send time on either side, naming the path and reason.

Frame metadata rides along verbatim: the full class vector (a tibble’s c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"), any class ending in "data.frame") and extra attributes such as a reference note or readr’s column specification cross opaquely — Python stashes them undecoded on the pymizu.Frame, and an unmodified echo restores them, so a pristine round trip is identical(). The stash rides the pristine received frame only: a frame rebuilt through pyarrow, polars, pandas, or from_arrow arrives in R as a plain data.frame — honest loss, never wrong labels. A named classed column (a named factor, Date, or POSIXct) and a column that is itself a labeled matrix stay declined, as do groupedData-style frames (a formula attribute is not portable) and data.table (its .internal.selfref pointer is not either).

Arrow data

The frame exchange extends to Arrow producers directly: an arrow Table, RecordBatch, or RecordBatchReader — and any struct-typed nanoarrow_array_stream or nanoarrow_array, which covers DBI::dbGetQueryArrow(), duckdb, adbc, and polars outputs — stages straight off the Arrow buffers, one layout write into the shared region rather than a conversion to R values first. The same path serves pools: an Arrow tabular returned from a task crosses as one frame region, and one nested in a payload — a list element, a task argument, the spliced task expression itself — crosses by reference as a frame leaf, the received object holding a view in place of the table. The receiver gets an ordinary data.frame, each column a view over the region’s pages, and mizu_as_arrow() converts back to Arrow: a struct-typed nanoarrow_array_stream whose buffers point straight into the shared region for attribute-free double, integer, integer64, and character columns, the rest (factors, Date / POSIXct / difftime, logical, raw) converting per column. A timestamp[ns] or duration[ns] column arrives as a POSIXct or difftime in seconds. The nanosecond counts cross verbatim, then convert to doubles with count * 1e-9 — the same conversion the µs-rounded form uses, so the values are identical bit for bit. Only sub-microsecond resolution is lost, rounded to double precision. A subset frame, or a new data frame assembled from received columns, also keeps the backing pages. The export borrows each column through its original region, and a column re-sent inside a new frame crosses by reference, not by copy. If a region’s producer exited, only that region’s columns fall back to the copy path. Two caveats: sending a stream consumes it — a streaming RecordBatchReader is fully materialized at send, source bytes and region resident at once — and fidelity is frame-level, not Arrow-schema-exact (a dictionary returns as a factor, uints widen, an int32 of INT32_MIN reads as NA, and a uint64 past 2^53 crosses as NA with a warning at send — firing on the worker for a pool publish, invisible to the submitter).

ch <- mizu_channel(quote(mizu_send(ch, mizu_recv(ch))))
mizu_send(ch, arrow::arrow_table(data.frame(x = runif(1e5), s = rep(c("a", "b", NA), length.out = 1e5))))

df <- mizu_recv(ch, timeout = 30)
stream <- mizu_as_arrow(df)
arrow::as_arrow_table(stream)
#> Table
#> 100000 rows x 2 columns
#> $x <double>
#> $s <large_string>

# a subset, or a new frame assembled from received columns, borrows the same pages
sub <- df["x"]
arrow::as_arrow_table(mizu_as_arrow(sub))
#> Table
#> 100000 rows x 1 columns
#> $x <double>
mixed <- data.frame(x = df$x, y = runif(1e5))
arrow::as_arrow_table(mizu_as_arrow(mixed))
#> Table
#> 100000 rows x 2 columns
#> $x <double>
#> $y <double>
mizu_close(ch)

The same bytes reach a Python peer as a pymizu.Frame, where pa.table(f) / pl.from_arrow(f) consume them with no export step at all.

Mixed-language pools

Channels move values; pools move computation — a pool’s workers can be Python processes, driven through a neutral task specification. mizu_py_pool_launcher() spawns them (python3 -m pymizu.worker, probed like the channel launcher), mizu_call() describes the task — a qualified "mod.fn" name or a .source = string, plus the constant arguments — and mizu_submit_call() stages it:

p <- mizu_pool(2L, launcher = mizu_py_pool_launcher())
t <- mizu_submit_call(p, mizu_call("numpy.quantile", runif(100), q = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75)))
mizu_collect(t)
#> [1] 0.2095956 0.4574587 0.6860231
s <- mizu_submit_call(p, mizu_call(.source = "y = x * 2\ny + 1", x = 20))
mizu_collect(s)
#> [1] 41
mizu_pool_stop(p)

Unnamed arguments map to the positional list and named ones to the named dict, matching Python’s *args, **kwargs; a .source = task evaluates in a fresh namespace with the named arguments bound as names and the result as the trailing expression’s value. The workers’ language comes from the pool itself — a plain mizu_submit() on a foreign pool errors locally naming mizu_submit_call(), a bare unqualified name errors at submit, and a non-portable argument raises mizu_error_not_portable at submit. Task errors cross as mizu_error_remote conditions with the remote type preserved, and a result without a portable home fails the task with one naming the type. Large arguments cross by reference rather than by copy: a fresh array past the zero-copy floor (32 KB) stages one layout write into a shared region and the worker reads a view over it, and an argument that is already a shared view (received from a channel, a pool result, or a mori::share()d vector) crosses as its identifier alone — a received view re-sent as an argument moves zero payload bytes. A pool whose workers predate the ref reader declines such arguments locally at submit, naming the remedy. The reverse direction mirrors: pymizu.Pool.create() with pymizu.r_pool_launcher(), and Pool.submit() with pymizu.call() specs.

The cross-language map

A spec is also mizu_map()’s .f — the cross-language map. The element fills the spec’s first positional slot (name kind) or binds as x (source kind), the spec’s own constants ride with it (so ... stays empty), and .template, .collect = "view", and .seed all work — the seed carrying as a neutral pair each worker language derives its own streams from, so invariance holds per worker language rather than identical draws across them:

p <- mizu_pool(2L, launcher = mizu_py_pool_launcher())
mizu_map(p, runif(6), mizu_call("numpy.quantile", q = c(0.25, 0.75)))
#> [[1]]
#> [1] 0.9576389 0.9576389
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] 0.1820563 0.1820563
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> [1] 0.03642347 0.03642347
#> 
#> [[4]]
#> [1] 0.6637499 0.6637499
#> 
#> [[5]]
#> [1] 0.228136 0.228136
#> 
#> [[6]]
#> [1] 0.6275008 0.6275008
mizu_map(p, runif(6), mizu_call("numpy.log"), .template = numeric(1))
#> [1] -1.8544914 -1.3848598 -0.5880317 -1.1311784 -0.1497597 -0.4560346
mizu_pool_stop(p)
